Few policies sound as unambiguously generous as free university tuition, yet the word 'free' conceals rather than answers the real question, which is who ought to pay for a degree. My view is that the state should carry a substantial share of the cost, but that abolishing fees for every student would be both regressive and, in the long run, self-defeating.

The case for public funding is stronger than its critics often admit. A degree does not merely raise one graduate's income; it produces doctors, teachers and engineers whose work benefits people who never set foot on a campus. Where those wider returns exist, it is reasonable for taxpayers to contribute, and where talented school leavers from poorer homes are deterred by the prospect of debt, society loses ability it can ill afford to waste.

The difficulty lies in the word 'all'. Students from affluent families are heavily over-represented at university almost everywhere, so a universal subsidy channels public money disproportionately towards those who need it least, and it does so partly through the taxes of people who left school at sixteen. Moreover, when governments foot the entire bill, they tend to control costs by rationing places or by allowing funding per student to erode quietly, with the result that free systems can end up admitting fewer disadvantaged applicants, not more.

A fairer settlement would separate the question of access from that of price. Means-tested grants could cover both fees and living costs for students from low-income households, while others would repay a contribution only once their earnings passed a set threshold, so that a graduate who never benefits financially from the degree never pays. Such a scheme keeps the door open without asking a care worker to subsidise a future surgeon.

In short, higher education deserves generous public investment, but making it free for everyone is a blunt instrument that serves the comfortable at least as well as the deserving. Targeted support achieves the stated aim more honestly.

Longer sentences have an obvious political appeal: they are cheap to announce, easy to understand and seem to promise that offenders will get what they deserve. As a strategy for reducing crime, however, they are among the least efficient tools available, and I disagree that they represent the best approach.

It is worth being precise about what prison can achieve. Locking up a persistent burglar or a violent offender prevents that person from harming the public for the duration of the sentence, and for a small group of dangerous individuals this protection justifies long terms. But the effect diminishes sharply as sentences lengthen, because most people commit crimes in their late teens and twenties and simply grow out of it. An extra five years imposed on a forty-year-old therefore buys very little additional safety at considerable public expense.

The deterrent argument is weaker still. It assumes that would-be offenders weigh up the likely penalty before acting, whereas a great deal of crime is impulsive, committed under the influence of drink or drugs, or carried out by people who are confident they will not be caught. What changes behaviour is the perceived likelihood of detection, not the theoretical severity of a punishment that may never arrive. Worse, longer spells inside tend to sever the ties that keep people law-abiding, such as a job, a tenancy and a family, so many prisoners are released more likely to reoffend than when they went in.

If the aim is genuinely fewer victims, the money spent on extending sentences would achieve more elsewhere: on visible, well-resourced policing that raises the chance of being caught, on drug treatment, and on education and employment schemes that give released prisoners a stake in staying out of trouble.

Prison has a necessary place in any justice system, but treating sentence length as the main lever confuses being seen to be tough with being effective.

The choice between building roads and improving public transport is often framed as a contest between drivers and everyone else, but it is better understood as a question of how a city uses scarce space. On that basis, I largely agree that public transport should take priority, although the argument applies far more strongly to cities than to the countryside.

The central problem with new urban roads is that they tend to defeat their own purpose. Extra lanes make driving temporarily quicker, which encourages more people to drive, and within a few years the new capacity is as congested as the old. A rail line does not suffer from this effect in the same way, since additional passengers make a service more viable rather than slower, and a single track can carry as many people as a motorway several times its width. For a growing city, the arithmetic of space alone makes mass transit the only option that can keep pace with demand.

There are wider gains as well. Frequent, reliable services give mobility to people who cannot drive, including teenagers, many older residents and those who simply cannot afford a car, and they reduce the emissions and noise that make dense neighbourhoods unpleasant to live in.

That said, it would be a mistake to treat road spending as inherently wasteful. Buses, delivery vans and ambulances all depend on roads, and in sparsely populated rural regions a regular bus service may cost far more per passenger than a well-maintained road. In such places, modest investment in roads, combined with on-demand minibuses, is the more realistic choice. Even in cities, maintaining existing roads is not the same as building new ones, and neglecting repairs would be a false economy.

On balance, then, governments should direct the bulk of new investment towards public transport in urban areas, while accepting that roads remain the backbone of mobility wherever populations are thin.

Predictions about artificial intelligence and employment tend to divide into two camps: one foresees mass redundancy, the other a wave of new occupations. Both, in my view, focus too narrowly on the total number of jobs, when the more pressing question is who will lose work, who will gain it, and how long the gap between the two will last.

Those who expect widespread unemployment have a stronger case than in previous technological shifts. Earlier machines mainly replaced physical effort, whereas current systems can draft contracts, summarise medical records and handle customer complaints, tasks once considered secure for educated workers. Because software can be copied and deployed almost instantly, the pace of change may outstrip the capacity of people in their forties and fifties to retrain, and a paralegal who loses her job is unlikely to become a machine-learning engineer.

The optimists, however, can point to a consistent historical pattern. Technologies that automate tasks usually lower the cost of a service, which increases demand for it and creates new roles around it. Spreadsheets did not eliminate accountants; they shifted the profession towards analysis and advice, and it grew. Something similar is already visible, as firms hire people to supervise, audit and apply AI tools in fields ranging from law to logistics.

I find the optimistic view more persuasive over a span of decades, but that is cold comfort to those displaced in the meantime. The new jobs will not necessarily appear in the same places, or be open to the same people, as those that disappear. Whether AI ultimately proves beneficial for employment will therefore depend less on the technology itself than on policy: on whether governments fund retraining that is genuinely accessible to mid-career workers, and whether safety nets can cushion the transition.

In short, AI is likely to create more work than it destroys, but only a deliberate effort will ensure that those who bear the cost also share in the gains.

The debate over remote work is often conducted as if there were a single right answer for every organisation. In reality, the question is less where people work than what kind of work they are doing and how far into their careers they are, and once it is framed that way, neither side is entirely right.

Advocates of working from home have a strong case on efficiency. Tasks that demand sustained concentration, such as writing code, analysing data or drafting a report, are frequently done better away from the interruptions of an open-plan office, and eliminating a long commute returns hours each week to employees. Employers benefit too, not only from lower overheads but from being able to recruit talented people regardless of where they live.

Those who favour the office, however, are right about something that productivity figures struggle to capture. Much of what junior staff learn is absorbed rather than taught: overhearing how a manager handles a difficult phone call, or asking a quick question that would feel too trivial to put in an email. Remote arrangements tend to suit experienced professionals who already have these skills and networks, while quietly slowing the development of newcomers. Offices also sustain the informal trust that makes collaboration across teams easier.

My own view is that a hybrid arrangement works best, but only if it is designed around purpose rather than attendance. Requiring everyone to come in on fixed days and then spend those days on video calls combines the drawbacks of both models. A better approach would reserve office time for activities that genuinely benefit from presence, such as mentoring, planning and solving problems as a team, and leave focused individual work to be done wherever people do it best. New recruits might reasonably spend more time on site than senior colleagues.

Ultimately, the office should be treated as a tool for particular kinds of work rather than a default location, and organisations that grasp this distinction will get the best from both arrangements.

Whenever a rocket launch dominates the headlines, someone inevitably asks why the money was not spent on hospitals instead. The question is reasonable, but it rests on the assumption that space exploration is a single activity, when in fact it ranges from weather satellites to symbolic crewed missions. Once that distinction is made, I believe most space spending is defensible, though not all of it.

Those who oppose it argue from urgency. A government that cannot guarantee clean water or timely surgery for its citizens, they say, has no business funding expeditions to distant planets, and the benefits of such missions are often speculative and decades away. This objection carries particular force in poorer countries, where launching a national space programme can look more like a bid for prestige than a response to public need.

Yet a large share of what is labelled 'space spending' is directed at problems on Earth. Satellites underpin weather forecasting, crop monitoring, navigation and the measurement of melting ice sheets; without them, governments would have far less reliable warning of typhoons or droughts. Robotic missions to other planets also yield knowledge about climate and geology that cannot be gained any other way, and at a fraction of the cost of sending people.

Where the critics are on firmer ground is with crewed exploration. Putting astronauts on the Moon or Mars costs vastly more than equivalent robotic work, largely because keeping humans alive in space is so demanding, and the scientific return per dollar is correspondingly lower. Such missions can inspire a generation, but inspiration is difficult to weigh against a waiting list for cancer treatment.

My conclusion, therefore, is that governments should continue to fund space activities that observe and protect our own planet, along with carefully chosen robotic science, while subjecting expensive crewed projects to far stricter scrutiny. The real choice is not between space and Earth, but between space spending that serves people on the ground and spending that mainly serves national pride.

In many households, children's only responsibility is to study, while parents quietly absorb the cooking, cleaning and laundry. I agree that children should be expected to share these tasks from an early age, but I would put the emphasis on why they do so: chores are valuable less as practical training than as a way of teaching children that a home is something everyone sustains.

The practical argument is the one most often made, and it is sound as far as it goes. A young adult who has never cooked a meal or used a washing machine faces an unnecessarily steep adjustment when leaving home, and these skills are rarely taught at school. Yet practical skills can be learned quickly at eighteen. What is much harder to acquire later is the underlying attitude, the habit of noticing that the bin is full and emptying it without being asked.

That attitude develops only when children's contribution is genuinely needed rather than symbolic. A five-year-old who sets the table each evening, or a twelve-year-old who is responsible for cooking one family meal a week, learns that other people depend on them and that domestic work, much of which is invisible, has to be done by somebody. This has implications beyond the family. Children who grow up assuming that someone else will always clean up after them may carry the same assumption into shared flats, workplaces and, eventually, their own relationships.

The main objection is that children today are under intense academic pressure and need every spare hour for study or rest. The concern is understandable, but most age-appropriate chores take a matter of minutes, and they offer a break from screens that many children would benefit from. The real risk lies in the opposite direction: raising high achievers who are helpless at home.

Requiring children to help is therefore justified, provided that tasks match their age and are presented as part of belonging to a family rather than as a punishment.

The question of whether news should be free online is often posed as a choice between access and quality. That framing is understandable, but it obscures a third possibility that I find more convincing: that some journalism should be paid for by readers, while the information citizens need to participate in public life should be free at the point of use, funded in other ways.

Advocates of free news start from a democratic principle. Voters cannot hold governments to account without reliable information, and if trustworthy reporting sits behind subscriptions, people who cannot or will not pay are left with whatever circulates freely, much of it partisan or simply false. A two-tier system of the informed and the misinformed would damage public debate for everyone, including subscribers.

Those who defend payment respond with an economic fact: serious reporting is expensive. An investigation into local government corruption may tie up several journalists and a lawyer for months and produce a single story. Since technology platforms captured most online advertising, the free, ad-funded model has rewarded content that attracts clicks quickly rather than reporting that takes time, and subscriptions have allowed some publications to rebuild newsrooms and answer to readers rather than to advertisers.

Both arguments are correct, which is why neither model works alone. Subscriptions sustain a handful of national titles well but are far less effective for local news, where the audience is too small to pay for coverage, and it is precisely at the local level that scrutiny of public institutions has declined most. For that kind of reporting, public interest funding, from independent foundations or publicly funded broadcasters, can fill the gap without making journalism dependent on whoever is in power.

My view, then, is that paying for news is both reasonable and necessary for in-depth journalism, but that essential public information should remain free to everyone. The aim should be a mix of funding models, since no single source of money can support all the journalism a democracy needs.

Holidaying at home, once seen as the option for those who could not afford anything better, has gained a certain prestige in recent years. I believe the trend is broadly positive, though its value depends on whether it spreads visitors across a country or simply concentrates them in a few famous places.

For travellers, the attractions are largely practical. Without visas, long-haul flights or currency charges, a trip can be planned at short notice and taken several times a year rather than saved for annually. This makes travel accessible to families who could never afford to go abroad, and it encourages people to discover regions of their own country that they might otherwise know only by name. A resident of a large city may have travelled to three foreign capitals yet never visited the mountains a few hours away.

The economic effects can be equally valuable. Spending by domestic tourists stays within the national economy and, when it reaches rural or coastal areas, can sustain guesthouses, restaurants and craft producers that would struggle on local demand alone. Domestic visitors also tend to be less sensitive to international events, so they provide a more stable base than foreign arrivals, as the tourism industry discovered during the pandemic. Shorter journeys, particularly by rail or road, usually mean lower emissions as well.

The disadvantages are worth taking seriously. Foreign travel offers an encounter with unfamiliar languages and ways of life that a domestic trip rarely provides, and a population that never leaves its own country may become more insular. More practically, when domestic demand fixes on the same few destinations, the result can be crowded beaches, rising prices and pressure on places with little infrastructure, while less famous regions see no benefit at all.

On balance, the advantages outweigh these drawbacks, particularly if tourism authorities actively promote a wider range of destinations. Exploring one's own country need not replace travel abroad; it can make people better informed about the place they come from before they go elsewhere.

Languages have always risen and declined, but the current rate of loss is unusual: many are spoken now only by elderly people whose grandchildren do not understand them. This matters for reasons that go beyond sentiment, and while not every language can be saved, much more could be done to protect those that remain.

The most immediate loss falls on the communities themselves. A language carries oral histories, songs, jokes and ways of addressing relatives that rarely survive translation intact. When it is no longer passed on, the break often runs through the middle of families, leaving grandparents unable to talk easily with their grandchildren and young people cut off from a part of their own identity. There is evidence that this sense of disconnection can affect wellbeing in indigenous communities, quite apart from the cultural loss.

There is also a loss for knowledge more broadly. Each language organises experience in its own way, and many encode detailed understanding of local plants, animals, seasons and landscapes. For linguists, every language that disappears without being documented removes evidence about the range of forms that human language can take, which can never be reconstructed afterwards.

The most important lesson from successful revivals is that a language survives only if children use it. Recording the last speakers is valuable but amounts to preservation rather than revival. What makes the difference is giving young people reasons and places to speak it: bilingual schooling from the earliest years, immersion nurseries where small children hear nothing else, and a presence in media, digital tools and public life that signals the language belongs to the present rather than the past. Official recognition matters because it changes that perception, as the revival of Welsh, Māori and Hebrew in different ways illustrates.

Ultimately, outsiders cannot save a language that its own speakers have decided to abandon. What governments can do is remove the pressures and stigma that drove the abandonment and give communities the resources to choose differently.

Public trust in scientists has not collapsed everywhere, but it has become more fragile and, in many countries, more divided along political lines. The causes lie partly in how information now circulates and partly in how science has been communicated, and restoring trust will require changes on both fronts.

The information environment is the most obvious factor. Online platforms reward content that provokes strong reactions, and a confident claim that a medicine is dangerous will usually travel further than a careful explanation of why it is safe. Because anyone can present themselves as an expert, the distinction between a researcher and a commentator with a large following has become blurred, and people tend to trust whoever shares their wider outlook. Once scientific questions such as climate change or vaccination become markers of political identity, evidence alone rarely changes minds.

Some of the damage, however, has been self-inflicted. During health crises, official advice has sometimes been presented with more certainty than the evidence allowed, so that later revisions looked like mistakes or deception rather than the normal process of science. Cases in which research funded by industry produced conveniently favourable results have also fed a suspicion that conclusions can be bought.

Rebuilding trust therefore means being more honest about uncertainty, not less. Scientists and health authorities should explain what is known, what is not yet known and what might change their advice, since a public prepared for revision is less likely to feel misled when it comes. Transparency about funding and the publication of data would answer the suspicion of hidden interests. In schools, teaching how scientific knowledge is produced, through testing, disagreement and correction, would matter more than memorising its results. Finally, trust tends to be local: doctors, teachers and community figures who explain evidence in familiar terms often persuade where national campaigns fail.

Trust in science cannot be demanded; it has to be earned through openness, and that includes openness about the limits of what science can say.
